title: GitHub - cookiengineer/qwen-reasoning-trainer: :rocket: Train Qwen3.8 with Reasoning Traces from other Teacher models
excerpt: :rocket: Train Qwen3.8 with Reasoning Traces from other Teacher models - cookiengineer/qwen-reasoning-trainer
content_html:
This is a Pure Go Abliteration, Reasoning Training, and Inference stack. It is implemented with a CPU backend and a Vulkan backend, which uses compute shaders and GPU kernels. It implements a complete GGUF/quant stack for the Qwen 3.8 27B model in its Q4_K_M GGUF quantization.

Motivation

This project aims to make Qwen3.8 self-training feasible for consumer-grade hardware, open source, for everyone to reproduce by themselves.

The Qwen Trainer project started as an experiment of making Qwen3.8 think like DeepSeek. The training pipeline meanwhile is reproducible and confirmed by others. The reason for doing so is that DeepSeek v4.1 Flash is very good at planning of coding tasks, but isn't good at cyber security or exploit validation tasks anymore because the model has been censored heavily compared to the previous DeepSeek v4 Pro model. As v4 Pro is now as overpriced as 'murican models, I decided to go this route.

The CPU backend kernel stack and the K/V cache implementations have been partially reused from my own experimental gonano SIMD model that focuses on better SIMD inference and scales with CPUs (but has its own limitations due to Go not having lower precisions than float32 available as of today, sadly).

Hardware Requirements

It is recommended to use the Qwen Reasoning Trainer stack with 48GB VRAM GPUs.

Abliteration, Reasoning Training, and Inference is tested actively on a machine with an AMD Radeon Pro W7800 48GB GPU and with 96GB DDR5 SODIMM CPU memory available. The costs for the hardware of self training a Qwen3.8 model is at a budget of around 5000 EUR, even in this ongoing RAM crisis.

Hardware requirements depend on the amount of context-length, the memory calculation is like this:

  • Around 17GB for the model weights
  • A couple of MB for GPU kernels (negligible)
  • Additional memory for K/V and cache

The K/V and cache require around ~10GB for 512k context length and around ~20GB for 1M context length.

That is why it's recommended to use a 32GB VRAM GPU for 512k context length, and a 48GB VRAM GPU for 1M context length. This allows to store everything inside the VRAM, so there's no latency caused by memory synchronization for each forward or backward run.

Software Requirements

  • Linux distributions only, as you might have guessed already (archlinux or debian recommended).
  • Go 1.27 (for build and tests).
  • The Vulkan glslc compiler and spirv-val to rebuild the SPIR-V shaders.
  • A Vulkan device for GPU acceleration and the GPU tests.
  • python3 with venv support only for the external verify-* tests.

Prerequisites

  1. Download the Qwen3.8-27B model from Hugging Face.

Unsloth Dynamic Q4_K_M quantization is the best model for this due to its weights-in-memory usage of around 17GB of VRAM.

Repository: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF

File: in the Files and versions list on the right side of the repo page, download Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf and place it at models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf. Alternatively let the CLI fetch the pinned artifact for you:

# Download the Qwen3.8 27B Q4_K_M model from huggingface:
./build/qwen-trainer download;
  1. Export the training data from your Opencode environment.

Use the session history as the teacher model's reasoning traces. The opencode-reasoning-extractor tool writes the following files for an exported dataset:

  • manifest.json
  • sft/<topic>/sessions.jsonl
  • sft/<topic>/turns.jsonl
  • subagents/<topic>/...
  • rl/metadata.jsonl.
# Export Reasoning Traces from your previous Opencode Sessions
opencode-reasoning-extractor ~/.local/share/opencode /path/to/qwen-reasoning-trainer/datasets/my-own-reasoning-traces;
  1. Point the Qwen Trainer at that output dataset directory using the --dataset CLI parameter.

Usage: Model and Dataset Interaction

# compile Vulkan compute shaders, then build the build/qwen-trainer binary
make;

# Command is always the first argument
# Flags (including --model) have to come afterwards

# Inspect the GGUF file for Tensor quantization details
./build/qwen-trainer inspect \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf;

# Run the Qwen Trainer as a quick generation test
./build/qwen-trainer run \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --prompt "The capital of France is" \
  --generate 8;

# Tokenize/validate the extractor output and report loss-mask statistics
./build/qwen-trainer dataset \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --dataset /path/to/my/own/reasoning-traces/from/opencode;
  • --model is required by every model command (inspect, run, abliterate, search, evaluate, dataset, train)
  • --dataset is repeatable. Use it multiple times to include multiple (exported) reasoning traces datasets

The compute backend defaults to auto: Vulkan is used when a device is present and has enough memory for the model, otherwise the CPU backend is used.

Override the compute backend with --backend auto|cpu|vulkan on the model commands. Use gpu-info to see the detected device and available memory.

Usage: Qwen Inference Server

The qwen-server exposes the same Vulkan/CPU inference pipeline through a minimal OpenAI-compatible API. You can build it with make server:

# Build inference server
make server;

# Execute inference server
./build/qwen-server --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf --port 8080;

The inference server is intentionally kept minimalistic. It serves the following endpoints:

  • GET /v1/models
  • POST /v1/chat/completions
  • GET /health.

Up to --max-concurrent requests are allowed at the same time. Each request has their own concurrency-safe Vulkan kernel running in-VRAM. Each vulkan kernel requires around 1MB of memory in-VRAM.

# Example request that returns ReasoningContent via HTTP Stream
curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}],
    "stream": true
  }';

Supported request features include stream (SSE), reasoning_content deltas, tools/tool_calls, temperature, top_p, top_k, seed, stop, max_tokens/max_completion_tokens, reasoning_effort, and chat_template_kwargs.

Thinking is enabled by default. Tool calls use the Qwen XML format and are returned as OpenAI API compatible tool_calls with JSON arguments.

Inference Flags

Flag Values Default
--device auto, cpu, vulkan auto
--context-length 128k, 256k, 384k, 512k (GGUF context)
--kv-cache-type q4_k, q8_0 q4_k
--max-concurrent (int) 1
--default-max-tokens (int) 1024
--speculative true, false true
--spec-draft-max (int) 4
--spec-draft-min-prob (float64) 0.6
--model-id (string) (GGUF filename)
--api-key (string)

Inference Environment Variables

Variable Description
QWEN_SERVER_MODEL Model GGUF Path
QWEN_SERVER_API_KEY Bearer API Key

On Vulkan the full kernel and inference forward shaders run in-VRAM on the GPU. The K/V are also stored in the quantized cache and appended with GPU shaders. The prefill chunk size is selected automatically from the context length and available device memory.

  • Streaming usage is included when stream_options.include_usage is true.
  • MTP speculative decoding is enabled by default on both Vulkan and CPU.
  • Context values above the natively supported GGUF context (256k) select YaRN automatically, with the factor derived from context / native_context.

See the ARCHITECTURE for more details.

Usage: Qwen Model Abliteration

The Qwen Trainer also removes the refusal/safety direction from the weights with Heretic-style directional ablation by using the same magnitude-preserving orthogonal ablation (called MPOA). It then optionally optimizes the ablation hyperparameters.

# 1. Abliterate with default parameters and write a new full Q4_K_M GGUF afterwards
./build/qwen-trainer abliterate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --out models/my-own-abliterated.gguf;

# 2. Search direction index and per-component weight kernels, and write the trial results.
./build/qwen-trainer search \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --trials 25 \
  --sampler tpe \
  --study models/search.jsonl \
  --out models/search-best.gguf;

# 3. Score the abliteration result via measuring refusal-keyword rate and KL divergence from base model
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/abliterated.gguf \
  --prompts source/prompts/heretic_harmful_test.jsonl \
  --max-tokens 32;

Prompt Sets and Prompt Limits

The prompts folder bundles the same datasets that Heretic uses behind the scenes, but the dataset has been pre-converted to JSON Lines where one object per line represents one question, essentially.

These prompts are embedded into the binary with go:embed, so that abliterate and search use them by default with no external files being needed.

Two bundled catalogs are selectable with --catalog:

Catalog Good prompts Bad prompts
heretic (default) general harmless instructions general harmful behaviors
cybersecurity defensive security questions offensive/dual-use questions

heretic is the default; pass --catalog heretic to select it explicitly.

# Use the cybersecurity catalog instead of the default Heretic set
./build/qwen-trainer abliterate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --catalog cybersecurity \
  --out models/Qwen3.8-27B-cyber-abliterated.gguf;

You can override individual sets with --good or --bad for abliterate and with --eval-good or --eval-bad for search. It would be heavily welcomed if you would contribute your custom abliteration questions catalog via Pull Request to this repository though!

The abliteration catalog files may be either plain text files (one prompt per line) or JSONL files. The --prompt-col CLI parameter selects the column, default text.

File Rows Role (default)
heretic_harmless_train.jsonl 25058 good prompts / residual directions (--good)
heretic_harmful_train.jsonl 416 bad prompts / residual directions (--bad)
heretic_harmless_test.jsonl 6265 KL divergence evaluation (--eval-good)
heretic_harmful_test.jsonl 104 refusal evaluation (--eval-bad)
cybersecurity_defensive_train.jsonl 2000 good prompts (--catalog cybersecurity)
cybersecurity_offensive_train.jsonl 2000 bad prompts (--catalog cybersecurity)
cybersecurity_defensive_test.jsonl 400 KL evaluation (--catalog cybersecurity)
cybersecurity_offensive_test.jsonl 400 refusal evaluation (--catalog cybersecurity)

The full files are quite large, so the limits are defaulted to Heretic's limits, with --limit 400 and --eval-limit 100. Set --limit 0 or --eval-limit 0 to use an entire file. Note that more prompts will cost one complete model forward, so abliteration time increases linearly.

Abliteration Flags

Flag Values (for) Commands Description
--catalog heretic, cybersecurity abliterate, search bundled prompt catalog (default heretic)
--no-device-residuals abliterate, search force host residual collection (debugging/parity)
--row-norm none, pre, full abliterate, search MPOA row normalization (default full)
--orthogonalize abliterate, search project the direction orthogonal to the good direction (default true)
--direction-index abliterate single global direction layer index (default -1 per layer)
--winsorize abliterate, search clamp residual components to a quantile in [0,1)
--sampler random, halton, tpe search optimizer (default random)
--lambda search KL weight in the objective refusal + lambda*KL (default 1.0)
--seed, --study search reproducible seed and resumable JSON Lines checkpoint

Note: the first-token for KL divergence measurement is a weak signal for a thinking model like this, because it emits <think> first. That's why small divergence scores are expected on short generations.

Usage: Qwen Abliteration Evaluation

evaluate scores a model along three independent axes; at least one input is required.

# Evaluates Refusal keyword rate and KL divergence from a base model
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/abliterated.gguf \
  --prompts source/prompts/heretic_harmful_test.jsonl \
  --max-tokens 32 \
  --base models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf;

# Evaluates Corpus Perplexity over a text file, scored in specified windows of N tokens
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --perplexity corpus.txt \
  --window 512;

# Evaluates multiple-choice accuracy over JSONL {context, choices, answer} records
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --tasks tasks.jsonl \
  --tasks-verbose;

The Corpus Perplexity evaluation uses non-overlapping windows and is defaulted to 512 tokens. Use --window 0 for the whole input. The window bounds peak memory at around vocab * window * 4 bytes, so it is the quality/memory limit and because it computes full LM-head logits for every window it is considerably slower per token than run.

The Task accuracy is scored by the length-normalized log-likelihood of each choice given the context. Use --tasks-normalize=false for raw sums.

Testing

The default suite is pure Go and needs neither a GPU nor Python:

make test;     # go test ./...
make check;    # fmt-check + vet + test (run this before calling anything done)

In order to run the suite on a remote GPU server, stream the working tree over SSH and run a make target there:

bash run-tests.sh my-48gb-vram-server;          # remote make check
bash run-tests.sh my-48gb-vram-server test;     # remote make test

The unit and end-to-end tests that need hardware or external data skip automatically. This means that make check works on any machine:

  • Vulkan tests skip when no device is present.
  • Real-model tests (tokenizer specials, example building) skip when no GGUF is present under models/.

External end-to-end verification tests

Independent cross-checks live under e2e-tests. Each end-to-end test has an isolated main program per check. They reuse reference implementations from other implementations and are never run directly by make check. Instead you have to run them like this (and they will install also python/cpp dependencies):

make verify-ref;    # Compares NumPy forward pass against the Go tiny model
make verify-data;   # Compares Jinja2 render of the model chat template and Python regex
make verify-quants; # Evaluates our quant implementations against llama.cpp's ggml-quants.c

Each of the end-to-end tests is also runnable directly. Execute them with the go -C flag, for example with go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-ref.

The Python references use a project-local virtualenv at source/e2e-tests/.venv, which is created on demand and installs dependencies from each test's own requirements.txt file. The venv itself is gitignored on purpose.

  • make e2e-venv creates the venv with all dependencies explicitly.
  • SYSTEM_PYTHON=python3.x selects the base interpreter used to build it.
  • E2E_PYTHON=/path/to/python runs the references against your own environment.

The verification programs can also be run directly with the QWEN38_REF_PYTHON environment variable:

QWEN38_REF_PYTHON=/path/to/python go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-ref;
QWEN38_REF_PYTHON=/path/to/python go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-data;
CC=/usr/bin/gcc go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-quants;

The reasoning traces dataset reader is additionally checked against an example fixture emitted by the opencode-reasoning-extractor's own writer.

License

This project is released under the MIT License. See LICENSE.txt for details.

They reuse reference implementations from other implementations and are never run directly by make check. Instead you have to run them like this (and they will install also python/cpp dependencies): make verify-ref; # Compares NumPy forward pass against the Go tiny model make verify-data; # Compares Jinja2 render of the model chat template and Python regex make verify-quants; # Evaluates our quant implementations against llama.cpp's ggml-quants.c Each of the end-to-end tests is also runnable directly. Execute them with the go -C flag, for example with go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-ref. The Python references use a project-local virtualenv at source/e2e-tests/.venv, which is created on demand and installs dependencies from each test's own requirements.txt file. The venv itself is gitignored on purpose. make e2e-venv creates the venv with all dependencies explicitly. SYSTEM_PYTHON=python3.x selects the base interpreter used to build it. E2E_PYTHON=/path/to/python runs the references against your own environment. The verification programs can also be run directly with the QWEN38_REF_PYTHON environment variable: QWEN38_REF_PYTHON=/path/to/python go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-ref; QWEN38_REF_PYTHON=/path/to/python go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-data; CC=/usr/bin/gcc go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-quants; The reasoning traces dataset reader is additionally checked against an example fixture emitted by the opencode-reasoning-extractor's own writer. content_html_zh:
This is a Pure Go Abliteration, Reasoning Training, and Inference stack. It is implemented with a CPU backend and a Vulkan backend, which uses compute shaders and GPU kernels. It implements a complete GGUF/quant stack for the Qwen 3.8 27B model in its Q4_K_M GGUF quantization.

动机

This project aims to make Qwen3.8 self-training feasible for consumer-grade hardware, open source, for everyone to reproduce by themselves.

The Qwen Trainer project started as an experiment of making Qwen3.8 think like DeepSeek. The training pipeline meanwhile is reproducible and confirmed by others. The reason for doing so is that DeepSeek v4.1 Flash is very good at planning of coding tasks, but isn't good at cyber security or exploit validation tasks anymore because the model has been censored heavily compared to the previous DeepSeek v4 Pro model. As v4 Pro is now as overpriced as 'murican models, I decided to go this route.

The CPU backend kernel stack and the K/V cache implementations have been partially reused from my own experimental gonano SIMD model that focuses on better SIMD inference and scales with CPUs (but has its own limitations due to Go not having lower precisions than float32 available as of today, sadly).

Hardware Requirements

It is recommended to use the Qwen Reasoning Trainer stack with 48GB VRAM GPUs.

Abliteration, Reasoning Training, and Inference is tested actively on a machine with an AMD Radeon Pro W7800 48GB GPU and with 96GB DDR5 SODIMM CPU memory available. The costs for the hardware of self training a Qwen3.8 model is at a budget of around 5000 EUR, even in this ongoing RAM crisis.

Hardware requirements depend on the amount of context-length, the memory calculation is like this:

  • Around 17GB for the model weights
  • A couple of MB for GPU kernels (negligible)
  • Additional memory for K/V and cache

The K/V and cache require around ~10GB for 512k context length and around ~20GB for 1M context length.

That is why it's recommended to use a 32GB VRAM GPU for 512k context length, and a 48GB VRAM GPU for 1M context length. This allows to store everything inside the VRAM, so there's no latency caused by memory synchronization for each forward or backward run.

Software Requirements

  • Linux distributions only, as you might have guessed already (archlinux or debian recommended).
  • Go 1.27 (for build and tests).
  • The Vulkan glslc compiler and spirv-val to rebuild the SPIR-V shaders.
  • A Vulkan device for GPU acceleration and the GPU tests.
  • python3 with venv support only for the external verify-* tests.

先决条件

  1. Download the Qwen3.8-27B model from Hugging Face.

Unsloth Dynamic Q4_K_M quantization is the best model for this due to its weights-in-memory usage of around 17GB of VRAM.

Repository: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF

File: in the Files and versions list on the right side of the repo page, download Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf and place it at models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf. Alternatively let the CLI fetch the pinned artifact for you:

# Download the Qwen3.8 27B Q4_K_M model from huggingface:
./build/qwen-trainer download;
  1. Export the training data from your Opencode environment.

Use the session history as the teacher model's reasoning traces. The opencode-reasoning-extractor tool writes the following files for an exported dataset:

  • 清单.json
  • sft/<topic>/sessions.jsonl
  • sft/<topic>/turns.jsonl
  • subagents/<topic>/...
  • rl/metadata.jsonl.
# Export Reasoning Traces from your previous Opencode Sessions
opencode-reasoning-extractor ~/.local/share/opencode /path/to/qwen-reasoning-trainer/datasets/my-own-reasoning-traces;
  1. Point the Qwen Trainer at that output dataset directory using the --dataset CLI parameter.

Usage: Model and Dataset Interaction

# compile Vulkan compute shaders, then build the build/qwen-trainer binary
make;

# Command is always the first argument
# Flags (including --model) have to come afterwards

# Inspect the GGUF file for Tensor quantization details
./build/qwen-trainer inspect \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf;

# Run the Qwen Trainer as a quick generation test
./build/qwen-trainer run \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --prompt "The capital of France is" \
  --generate 8;

# Tokenize/validate the extractor output and report loss-mask statistics
./build/qwen-trainer dataset \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --dataset /path/to/my/own/reasoning-traces/from/opencode;
  • --model is required by every model command (inspect, run, abliterate, search, evaluate, dataset, train)
  • --dataset is repeatable. Use it multiple times to include multiple (exported) reasoning traces datasets

The compute backend defaults to auto: Vulkan is used when a device is present and has enough memory for the model, otherwise the CPU backend is used.

Override the compute backend with --backend auto|cpu|vulkan on the model commands. Use gpu-info to see the detected device and available memory.

Usage: Qwen Inference Server

The qwen-server exposes the same Vulkan/CPU inference pipeline through a minimal OpenAI-compatible API. You can build it with make server:

# Build inference server
make server;

# Execute inference server
./build/qwen-server --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf --port 8080;

The inference server is intentionally kept minimalistic. It serves the following endpoints:

  • 获取/v1/模型
  • POST /v1/聊天/完成
  • 获取/健康。

Up to --max-concurrent requests are allowed at the same time. Each request has their own concurrency-safe Vulkan kernel running in-VRAM. Each vulkan kernel requires around 1MB of memory in-VRAM.

# Example request that returns ReasoningContent via HTTP Stream
curl -N http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 2+2?"}],
    "stream": true
  }';

Supported request features include stream (SSE), reasoning_content deltas, tools/tool_calls, temperature, top_p, top_k, seed, stop, max_tokens/max_completion_tokens, reasoning_effort, and chat_template_kwargs.

Thinking is enabled by default. Tool calls use the Qwen XML format and are returned as OpenAI API compatible tool_calls with JSON arguments.

Inference Flags

Flag 价值观 默认
--device auto, cpu, vulkan auto
--context-length 128k, 256k, 384k, 512k (GGUF context)
--kv-cache-type q4_k, q8_0 q4_k
--max-concurrent (int) 1
--default-max-tokens (int) 1024
--speculative true, false true
--spec-draft-max (int) 4
--spec-draft-min-prob (float64) 0.6
--model-id (string) (GGUF filename)
--api-key (string)

Inference Environment Variables

多变的 描述
QWEN_SERVER_MODEL Model GGUF Path
QWEN_SERVER_API_KEY Bearer API Key

On Vulkan the full kernel and inference forward shaders run in-VRAM on the GPU. The K/V are also stored in the quantized cache and appended with GPU shaders. The prefill chunk size is selected automatically from the context length and available device memory.

  • Streaming usage is included when stream_options.include_usage is true.
  • MTP speculative decoding is enabled by default on both Vulkan and CPU.
  • Context values above the natively supported GGUF context (256k) select YaRN automatically, with the factor derived from context / native_context.

See the ARCHITECTURE for more details.

Usage: Qwen Model Abliteration

The Qwen Trainer also removes the refusal/safety direction from the weights with Heretic-style directional ablation by using the same magnitude-preserving orthogonal ablation (called MPOA). It then optionally optimizes the ablation hyperparameters.

# 1. Abliterate with default parameters and write a new full Q4_K_M GGUF afterwards
./build/qwen-trainer abliterate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --out models/my-own-abliterated.gguf;

# 2. Search direction index and per-component weight kernels, and write the trial results.
./build/qwen-trainer search \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --trials 25 \
  --sampler tpe \
  --study models/search.jsonl \
  --out models/search-best.gguf;

# 3. Score the abliteration result via measuring refusal-keyword rate and KL divergence from base model
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/abliterated.gguf \
  --prompts source/prompts/heretic_harmful_test.jsonl \
  --max-tokens 32;

Prompt Sets and Prompt Limits

The prompts folder bundles the same datasets that Heretic uses behind the scenes, but the dataset has been pre-converted to JSON Lines where one object per line represents one question, essentially.

These prompts are embedded into the binary with go:embed, so that abliterate and search use them by default with no external files being needed.

Two bundled catalogs are selectable with --catalog:

目录 Good prompts Bad prompts
heretic (default) general harmless instructions general harmful behaviors
cybersecurity defensive security questions offensive/dual-use questions

heretic is the default; pass --catalog heretic to select it explicitly.

# Use the cybersecurity catalog instead of the default Heretic set
./build/qwen-trainer abliterate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --catalog cybersecurity \
  --out models/Qwen3.8-27B-cyber-abliterated.gguf;

You can override individual sets with --good or --bad for abliterate and with --eval-good or --eval-bad for search. It would be heavily welcomed if you would contribute your custom abliteration questions catalog via Pull Request to this repository though!

The abliteration catalog files may be either plain text files (one prompt per line) or JSONL files. The --prompt-col CLI parameter selects the column, default text.

File Rows Role (default)
heretic_harmless_train.jsonl 25058 good prompts / residual directions (--good)
heretic_harmful_train.jsonl 416 bad prompts / residual directions (--bad)
heretic_harmless_test.jsonl 6265 KL divergence evaluation (--eval-good)
heretic_harmful_test.jsonl 104 refusal evaluation (--eval-bad)
cybersecurity_defensive_train.jsonl 2000 good prompts (--catalog cybersecurity)
cybersecurity_offensive_train.jsonl 2000 bad prompts (--catalog cybersecurity)
cybersecurity_defensive_test.jsonl 400 KL evaluation (--catalog cybersecurity)
cybersecurity_offensive_test.jsonl 400 refusal evaluation (--catalog cybersecurity)

The full files are quite large, so the limits are defaulted to Heretic's limits, with --limit 400 and --eval-limit 100. Set --limit 0 or --eval-limit 0 to use an entire file. Note that more prompts will cost one complete model forward, so abliteration time increases linearly.

Abliteration Flags

Flag 价值观 (for) Commands 描述
--catalog heretic, cybersecurity abliterate, search bundled prompt catalog (default heretic)
--no-device-residuals abliterate, search force host residual collection (debugging/parity)
--row-norm none, pre, full abliterate, search MPOA row normalization (default full)
--orthogonalize abliterate, search project the direction orthogonal to the good direction (default true)
--direction-index abliterate single global direction layer index (default -1 per layer)
--winsorize abliterate, search clamp residual components to a quantile in [0,1)
--sampler random, halton, tpe 搜索 optimizer (default random)
--lambda 搜索 KL weight in the objective refusal + lambda*KL (default 1.0)
--seed, --study 搜索 reproducible seed and resumable JSON Lines checkpoint

Note: the first-token for KL divergence measurement is a weak signal for a thinking model like this, because it emits <think> first. That's why small divergence scores are expected on short generations.

Usage: Qwen Abliteration Evaluation

evaluate scores a model along three independent axes; at least one input is required.

# Evaluates Refusal keyword rate and KL divergence from a base model
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/abliterated.gguf \
  --prompts source/prompts/heretic_harmful_test.jsonl \
  --max-tokens 32 \
  --base models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf;

# Evaluates Corpus Perplexity over a text file, scored in specified windows of N tokens
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --perplexity corpus.txt \
  --window 512;

# Evaluates multiple-choice accuracy over JSONL {context, choices, answer} records
./build/qwen-trainer evaluate \
  --model models/Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --tasks tasks.jsonl \
  --tasks-verbose;

The Corpus Perplexity evaluation uses non-overlapping windows and is defaulted to 512 tokens. Use --window 0 for the whole input. The window bounds peak memory at around vocab * window * 4 bytes, so it is the quality/memory limit and because it computes full LM-head logits for every window it is considerably slower per token than run.

The Task accuracy is scored by the length-normalized log-likelihood of each choice given the context. Use --tasks-normalize=false for raw sums.

测试

The default suite is pure Go and needs neither a GPU nor Python:

make test;     # go test ./...
make check;    # fmt-check + vet + test (run this before calling anything done)

In order to run the suite on a remote GPU server, stream the working tree over SSH and run a make target there:

bash run-tests.sh my-48gb-vram-server;          # remote make check
bash run-tests.sh my-48gb-vram-server test;     # remote make test

The unit and end-to-end tests that need hardware or external data skip automatically. This means that make check works on any machine:

  • Vulkan tests skip when no device is present.
  • Real-model tests (tokenizer specials, example building) skip when no GGUF is present under models/.

External end-to-end verification tests

Independent cross-checks live under e2e-tests. Each end-to-end test has an isolated main program per check. They reuse reference implementations from other implementations and are never run directly by make check. Instead you have to run them like this (and they will install also python/cpp dependencies):

make verify-ref;    # Compares NumPy forward pass against the Go tiny model
make verify-data;   # Compares Jinja2 render of the model chat template and Python regex
make verify-quants; # Evaluates our quant implementations against llama.cpp's ggml-quants.c

Each of the end-to-end tests is also runnable directly. Execute them with the go -C flag, for example with go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-ref.

The Python references use a project-local virtualenv at source/e2e-tests/.venv, which is created on demand and installs dependencies from each test's own requirements.txt file. The venv itself is gitignored on purpose.

  • make e2e-venv creates the venv with all dependencies explicitly.
  • SYSTEM_PYTHON=python3.x selects the base interpreter used to build it.
  • E2E_PYTHON=/path/to/python runs the references against your own environment.

The verification programs can also be run directly with the QWEN38_REF_PYTHON environment variable:

QWEN38_REF_PYTHON=/path/to/python go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-ref;
QWEN38_REF_PYTHON=/path/to/python go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-data;
CC=/usr/bin/gcc go -C source run ./e2e-tests/verify-quants;

The reasoning traces dataset reader is additionally checked against an example fixture emitted by the opencode-reasoning-extractor's own writer.
